extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and general readers interested in political economy
extracted.subtask_short: economic analysis of corporations and labour
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th‑century political‑economy exposition describing how corporations, apprenticeship statutes, public charities, trade regulation, and poor‑law settlements shape the distribution of wages, profits, and the mobility of labour and capital between towns and country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship system as a barrier to free competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The system of long unpaid apprenticeships restrains free competition by excluding potential competitors and thereby maintains higher prices and wages for incumbents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts the present long apprenticeship with an alternative where young men would work as paid journeymen and pay for spoilt materials; such an arrangement would make education more effectual and cheaper for society but would reduce wages and profits by increasing competition. Tradeoffs between education quality, cost, and post‑training wages are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations established to prevent price reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations and corporation laws are instituted chiefly to prevent reduction of price (and thus of wages and profit) by restraining free competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: in many parts of Europe a town corporate sufficed to erect a corporation, while in England a royal charter was often required (frequently granted upon payment). Corporations inspect their own bye‑laws; their powers enable members to limit competition and protect prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation regulations advantage towns over the country
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations enacted by town corporations allow town inhabitants (traders and artificers) to buy from one another somewhat dearer while selling to the country at higher prices, giving towns a net advantage over the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because towns draw subsistence and materials from the country and pay for them chiefly by exporting manufactured goods, anything that increases town wages and profits lets towns purchase more cheaply from the country, breaking natural equality between town and country commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: High duties and restrictions protect urban industry from foreign competition
rubrics_metrics.description: High duties on foreign manufactures and restrictions on alien merchants serve the same purpose as corporation laws: they protect town industries from foreign competition, with the cost ultimately borne by country landlords, farmers, and labourers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protectionist regulations, together with corporation privileges, enable town producers to raise prices without fear of being undersold by countrymen or foreigners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration in towns leads to greater rewards for industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry carried on in towns is generally more advantageous than that of the country because stock and labour naturally seek the most profitable employment, concentrating in towns and yielding higher wages and profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation: more self‑made fortunes arise from trade and manufactures (town industry) than from improvement of land; over time accumulated urban stock may overflow into the country, raising rural wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation spirit and voluntary combinations facilitate anti‑competitive behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absent formal incorporation, the ‘corporation‑spirit’—jealousy of strangers, aversion to apprentices, secretive practices—induces voluntary associations that prevent free competition (e.g., refusing apprentices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small trades are especially prone: a few wool‑combers can control employment for many spinners and weavers by refusing apprentices or otherwise restricting entry, effectively enslaving the larger manufacture to the handful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer discipline, not corporate discipline, ensures workmanship quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The real and effectual discipline over a workman is that exercised by his customers; exclusive corporations weaken this discipline because members are guaranteed employment regardless of behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: in many incorporated towns tolerable workmen are scarce; better work is found in suburbs where workmen lack exclusive privileges and must rely on reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws facilitating trade assemblies foster collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations that make it easy for members of the same trade to assemble (public registers of names/addresses, common funds for the poor/sick, compulsory incorporation) facilitate conspiracies to raise prices and limit competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific mechanisms: public registers connect otherwise unknown individuals; common charitable funds create joint management interests; incorporation makes majority decisions binding on all members, enabling long‑lasting, enforceable restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public funding of professional education increases competition and lowers rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Pensions, scholarships, exhibitions, and other public or charitable funding that educate many people for a profession draw more people into that profession than the market can reward, depressing pecuniary recompense for its practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: education of churchmen, lawyers, physicians, and men of letters—when largely publicly funded—leads to oversupply and low pay for many practitioners; this can degrade the standing and pecuniary rewards of the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological and institutional change alters occupational rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovations such as the art of printing changed how men of letters earn a living, increasing the number who write for bread and changing the relative rewards between teaching and authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before printing, eminent teachers earned high fees and teaching was a principal occupation for men of letters; printing created new, often lower‑paid forms of literary employment that affected market rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on mobility of labour and stock produce inconvenient inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes of apprenticeship, exclusive corporate privileges, and poor‑law settlement rules obstruct the free circulation of labour (between employments and places) and of stock, causing mismatches where some occupations are oversupplied while others lack labour or capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: similar manufactures (e.g., plain linen, plain silk, plain woollen weaving) could shift labour between them if not for legal barriers; obstruction keeps workers from moving to thriving trades and forces them onto poor relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor‑law settlement rules impede poor people's movement
rubrics_metrics.description: English poor‑law rules (e.g., settlement by forty days' residence, requirements to give written notice and publication, and additional means of settlement) make gaining a new settlement difficult and obstruct poor people's ability to establish themselves in new parishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical progression: 43 Elizabeth made parishes responsible for their own poor; subsequent statutes (Charles II, James II, William III) modified how residence and notice operate. Practical routes to settlement (taxation, parish office, apprenticeship, year’s service) are largely unavailable to the very poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal attempts to regulate wages are generally ineffectual
rubrics_metrics.description: When laws attempt to fix or regulate wages (either to raise curates' wages or lower workmen's), they frequently fail because individuals will accept less due to indigence or receive more due to competing demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: historical wage comparisons show variations; statute efforts (e.g., to raise curates' pay) often do not achieve intended effects because of market forces and individual willingness to accept lower pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequal educational financing distorts entry and rewards across professions
rubrics_metrics.description: When one profession's education is publicly funded while others' are privately paid, supply differences distort competition and rewards: publicly funded professions become crowded and underpaid, while privately funded professions retain higher pecuniary rewards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative examples: many men of letters and clergy educated at public expense depressed rewards for teachers and other learned professions; law and physic (medicine), if publicly funded en masse, would see their pecuniary rewards greatly reduced.
